newsitem.title: UK: Redwood seeks to keep UK Conservatives together.
newsitem.headline: Redwood seeks to keep UK Conservatives together.

text.p: Right-wing Conservative John Redwood on Tuesday denied that the party would split if he won the election for its leadership now getting under way.

"I don't want a sectional party, a factional party, a party obsessed by only one issue," Redwood, known for his opposition to a single European currency, told a news conference to announce he would be a candidate to replace John Major.
"I believe the Conservative Party is a broad church. It must stay a broad church. The trouble is we don't have enough worshippers at the moment," Redwood added.
Redwood is the third Conservative to announce his candidature after outgoing Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, a moderate, and former Social Security Secretary Peter Lilley, a right-winger.

He said the Conservatives, shattered by their worst general election result for 150 years last week, needed to regroup by concentrating on issues such as education, the health service and the economy, and by pursuing success in local government.

He said he was well placed to provide the leadership for the fight-back because he had been out of ministerial office for two years before the election -- he resigned as Welsh Secretary in 1995 to challenge Major for the party leadership.
"Against (Prime Minister) Tony Blair across the despatch box, I would not have to defend every last deed of the 1992-7 government, and could look forward," he said.
Redwood insisted he would be able to cooperate with outgoing Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke in opposition despite their differences of approach to Brussels.
He said, for instance, that on the question of the single currency, both he and Clarke agreed "a fudged single currency would be a disaster for both Britain and the rest of Europe".
Redwood said a fudged currency was likely to prove to be the only one on offer. -- London Newsroom +44 171 5427767
